title: Pyrography bird outline panel
subtitle: Pyrography: a simple bird silhouette burned on a lime wood panel
excerpt: A single bird silhouette burned onto a 15 cm square lime wood panel, a first pyrography project for learning consistent line pressure, pen speed, and working from a transferred design. Lime wood is the best beginner pyrography timber: even-grained, light-coloured, and it burns cleanly at low to medium temperature.
sourceNotes: Cassell's Book of Drawing and Design (1899) for the silhouette transfer technique; standard pyrography method from Cassell's Cyclopaedia of Mechanics vol. III (1885).

glossaryTerms.definition: The technique of burning designs into wood using a heated metal tip. From the Greek pyro (fire) and graphos (writing).
Carbon-coated paper used to transfer a drawn design to a wood surface by tracing over it with a pen or stylus.

content.text: A bird outline panel is a first
pyrography
project. Transfer a design to a flat panel and burn it at steady speed. The skills practised here, line pressure and heat control, carry through to all later pyrography work.
Before you start burning.
Ventilation: pyrography produces wood smoke. Work near an open window or use a fume extractor. Do not burn in an enclosed room.
Hot tip: a pyrography pen tip is as hot as a soldering iron (200, 400 °C). Never touch the tip. Set the pen down on its stand when not actively burning, not on the workbench surface.
Fire: keep the pyrography unit and workpiece clear of flammable materials. Do not leave the unit unattended when switched on.
First aid: a burn from a pyrography tip is a contact burn. Run under cool water for 20 minutes. Do not apply ice or butter. Burns larger than a 5p coin go to A&E.
What you need
Wood

One seasoned lime wood panel, 15 cm × 15 cm, 8, 12 mm thick. Lime (Tilia) is the standard pyrography wood: pale, even-grained, and it burns cleanly at all temperatures without creating areas of hard and soft grain contrast (as oak and pine do). Sand the surface to 240 grit before burning.
Tools
Pyrography pen, fixed wire-tip type, with a fine ball tip or writing tip.
Transfer paper (carbon paper) and a printed or drawn bird reference image.
Sandpaper 240 grit for the panel preparation.
Pencil for the transfer and a ruler for positioning.
Preparing the panel
Sand the lime panel to 240 grit, going with the grain. Remove all dust with a dry cloth. The surface must be clean and smooth, any scratches become permanent burn marks.
Transferring the design
Place the
transfer paper

carbon-side down on the panel. Position the bird reference image on top. Secure both layers with tape at the corners. Trace over the bird outline firmly with a pencil or ballpoint pen. Lift the corner to check the transfer is crisp before removing. The transferred line should be faint, just visible enough to follow with the pen, but not so dark that it shows through the burn.
Setting the temperature

Start at a low temperature setting, typically 3, 4 on a 1, 10 fixed-tip pen unit. Test on a scrap piece of the same timber: a light tan line with no smoke is correct for line work. Increase by one step at a time until the pen leaves a clean, consistent line. Lime burns at a lower temperature than most hardwoods; a setting that works on pine will be too hot for lime.
Burning the outline

Hold the pen like a pencil, at about 45 degrees to the surface. Move the pen slowly and steadily along the transferred line. Speed determines the depth of colour: slow = dark; fast = light. Keep speed consistent throughout each stroke. On curves, rotate the panel rather than changing the pen angle. The outside contour of the bird is burned first; any inside detail lines after. Do not try to darken a line by pressing harder, increase the temperature instead.
Finishing

After burning, wipe the panel with a barely damp cloth to remove any carbon residue. Do not sand the burned lines. Apply one thin coat of beeswax or clear wood wax to protect the surface and deepen the contrast between the pale wood and the burn marks. Allow to dry and buff.

attrs.symptom: The burned line is uneven, darker in some places and barely visible in others
attrs.cause: Pen speed varied along the stroke; or the tip temperature changed as the pen heated up
attrs.fix: Allow the pen to heat up fully before starting (1, 2 minutes after switch-on). Practise on scrap with the goal of a consistent speed that matches the temperature setting. If speed is the issue, move slightly faster at the beginning of each stroke when the line is going dark.
